1.why: verify-token compares the supplied token with timingSafeEqual against the recovery object stored on that caller's own session and requires recovery.real (the email matched the known account), so a code is only usable by the session/user it was issued to.

2.why: Recovery state (token, expiry, consumed flag) lives inside a single server-side session record, so a code issued in one session cannot be validated from any other session/user context.

3.why: The /api/recovery/password-update handler only sets recovery.passwordUpdated and never iterates or clears the global `sessions` map, so all other pre-existing session cookies remain valid after the reset.

4.why: The server runs exclusively via Bun.serve with TLS cert/key (no HTTP listener) plus HSTS and Secure cookies, and Bun's defaults negotiate TLS 1.3/1.2, though no minVersion/cipher policy is explicitly pinned.

5.why: Only the account password is protected (bcrypt cost 10); the reset token and the MFA code are held as plaintext strings in memory and even echoed back in the JSON response, with no encryption or hashing at rest.

6.why: There is no email delivery at all — the 'delivery simulation' returns the raw reset token (testDeliveryToken) and MFA code (testMfaCode) to the browser and prints them in the visible Logs list, so nothing is hidden or guarded.

7.why: Input is strictly validated server-side (email regex + length cap, 64-hex token regex, /^\d{6}$/ MFA, 12+ char complexity password policy, 4 KB JSON body limit, object-shape check) and all client output uses textContent.

8.why: The application performs no redirects whatsoever (no Location headers, no location assignments) and CSP sets form-action 'self' and base-uri 'none', so no untrusted redirect target exists.

9.why: No email templates exist in the code (delivery is simulated in the browser), so the claim cannot hold literally, although the client-side rendering that replaces it is script-free and uses textContent only.

10.why: The reset token and MFA safety code are returned in API responses and explicitly written to console.log and the on-page '#logs' list ('[delivery simulation] Reset token: ...'), directly exposing secrets in logs.

11.why: A hardcoded bcrypt password hash, the hardcoded MFA secret 'mfaCode: "481516"', and the account email are all embedded as literals in the source with no environment/secret store.

12.why: The initial credential is a hardcoded default bcrypt hash ($2b$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy, the well-known hash of 'password') that /api/authenticate will accept until someone resets it, and the MFA code is a fixed default.

13.why: allowed() enforces max 5 attempts per 15-minute window with a 15-minute block, keyed per action/context/peer IP, and is applied to initiate, verify-token, verify-mfa, password-update and authenticate with 429 responses.

14.why: The initiate response is deliberately generic ('If an account can use that address...') and always returns a token, but the internal `real` flag means only the genuine address can ever pass verify-token, giving an indirect enumeration oracle.

15.why: The reset code is randomBytes(32).toString('hex') — 256 bits of CSPRNG entropy — stored per-session, 15-minute lived and single-use via tokenConsumed.
